turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Carmel Byrne? Come on in, we'll do the checks before Dr. O'Sullivan sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah grand, thanks. I was half afraid I'd missed you, the bus was late and then the rain started, and I had to go back for the umbrella, so I'm a bit flustered.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're grand, you're here. Sit up on the chair and I'll get the blood pressure.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The left arm is easier, the right one plays up if you pump it too hard. I don't know why, it just does.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Left it is. Blood pressure is 146 over 88, and your pulse is 78.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): 146, is it. That's up a shade on what I get at home, though the home yoke is old.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature is 36.7, oxygen saturations 97 percent, and you're breathing at 16.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel warm in the bed at night but I don't think I've had a temperature, not since the flu anyway. I checked with the little thermometer and it was normal.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Weight today is 64.5 kilograms.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that all? I won't argue with the scales, I suppose. Will the doctor be long?
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): He's just finishing. While we wait, the repeat list says bendroflumethiazide 2.5 milligrams, one in the morning, the water tablet.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not what I take. It's the water tablet all right, the little white one for the blood pressure, but I'm on five milligrams. The doctor in Ennis changed it. I'm certain it was five.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): The screen says two point five. We'll leave that for himself to sort, I won't change it here.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): And I use the purple inhaler as well, for the asthma, two puffs in the morning and two at night, I never miss that one. The box says Seretide, if that's what you're writing.
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Seretide, twice a day, grand. Any other tablets?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I was taking paracetamol, two tablets four times a day, when the flu was on me, and those Lemsip sachets at night. I stopped the both of them when the shivers went, a good while back.
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): Allergies on the chart are blank. Any medicines that don't suit you?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, my mother used to say penicillin, that I came out in something as a child, but I never saw it myself and nobody ever wrote it down. I wouldn't swear to it.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carmel, sorry to keep you. I'm Dr. O'Sullivan. You've been coughing, is that the main of it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): It is, yeah. I'm after having this cough six weeks now. It came on after the flu, and it's worse at night, desperate worse, I'm waking himself with it.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks, after a flu. Tell me about the flu first, when that started.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the thing, I cannot put a date on the flu at all. It was after the Christmas, or maybe into January, the days all blended, last winter or — no, not last winter, this winter just gone, but I couldn't tell you the week.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, we won't force a date. The cough you're happier calling six weeks.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The cough, yes, six weeks, I'd nearly swear to that because my sister's birthday was in the middle of it and I couldn't sing. The flu itself, the aches and the fever, that's gone.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the cough, or pain in the chest?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood, thank God, and no chest pain. It's a dry enough cough at night, and then in the morning there's a small bit of white phlegm, not much.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathless with it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs, a bit, if I'm carrying the messages. On the flat I'm grand. I have the asthma years, so I know that feeling, and this is a cousin of it but not the same.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Night sweats, or fever now?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweats, and no fever now. I said that to the nurse. And before you ask, I haven't lost weight. The appetite is grand, I'm eating the dinners.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any travel lately, abroad, or anyone around you with tuberculosis?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No travel. I haven't been out of Clare, only to Limerick for the Christmas shopping. And no, nobody with TB. I wouldn't be near that.

[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, I should say — her brother rang the desk while she was on the way in. He said their cousin Aoife was treated for TB in the spring, and that Carmel stayed in the house with her a weekend.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah now, that's not it at all. Aoife had a chest infection, they never said TB to me, and I did not stay the weekend. I haven't been in that house since the wedding, and that's years ago. My brother gets things mixed.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): So you're saying no contact, and he's saying there was. I can't settle that from here. We'll note both and not pretend we know.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Please do, because I'd hate a wrong thing on the file. He's a worrier, always was, even as a boy he'd ring people.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to the chest. Deep breath.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, I always cough when you do that. There, that's the one.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Throat looks quiet, no big nodes in the neck. The lungs are clear of crackles. There's a soft wheeze at the right base, not much.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The right side is where I feel it tickle at night, so that fits, I suppose.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the waterworks, the bowels, any of that playing up?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No, all grand that way. I go as usual. I drink plenty of tea, maybe too much, my husband gives out about the teabags.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the smoking?

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I smoked in my twenties, twenty a day, silly, and I gave it up when I was expecting the first child. Not a cigarette since. I don't drink much either, a glass of wine on a Sunday if there's a match on.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): You live with your husband, you said.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I do, Tom, and the dog. I do three mornings in the charity shop in Ennis, folding clothes, nothing heavy. Or I did, until this cough made me mortified, coughing over the jumpers.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): The asthma, is that still on the books, and the blood pressure?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, yes. Asthma since I was, oh I couldn't tell you, my forties or maybe before, the year is gone from me. Blood pressure they've had me on the water tablet for, five years or thereabouts.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you're sure the water tablet is five milligrams, not the two point five on our list.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm sure. Well — I'm nearly sure. The box at home might say two point five and I take two of them? No. I take one tablet. I think the tablet is five. I should have brought the box. I always mean to and I never do.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): So we don't actually have a settled dose. I'm not going to rewrite it today on a hunch.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fair. I'll bring the box next time. It's in the press beside the kettle, I can see it in my head and still I left it.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Back to the cough. You said no weight loss, and the appetite is good.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I did say that. But actually, now that I'm standing here, the trousers are loose. I've had to pull the belt in a notch. I don't know when that started, last month or before Christmas, I couldn't date it. So maybe I have dropped a bit, even with the dinners.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Loose clothes, but you can't time it. I'm not going to hang a cause on that on its own.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want you saying the worst thing either. I googled, which I know is stupid, and then I closed the laptop. My neighbour had a bad lung and I got a fright, that's all.

[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm turning it over in my head and there are a few directions it could go, but I'm not going to name a cause today. The film has to come first, and I won't dress a guess up as an answer.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do we do, then? I can't be coughing through the charity shop all spring.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll order a chest X-ray. That one is happening, the desk will book it this week.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that the one where you stand against the plate? I had one years ago for a visa, or was it a visa, maybe it was the insurance. Anyway I can do that.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, standing film. If it doesn't explain the cough, or if you're no better when we look again, we might do a CT scan, but not now.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): A scan only if we need it. Grand. I don't fancy extra trips if the X-ray is enough.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep using the purple inhaler the way you are, two and two. Don't start any new cough bottle from the chemist on top of it.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): I nearly bought one yesterday, a brown one, I don't even know the name, and then I put it back. So I never took that.
[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good that you didn't. If you cough up blood, or you get properly breathless at rest, or a fever comes back, don't wait on me, come in or go to the local emergency.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I will, I promise. Tom will make me, he's already giving out that I left it six weeks.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in two weeks with the X-ray, whether you feel better or not. Not an if, a definite appointment.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, even if I'm grand. I'll write it on the calendar so I don't mix it up with the dentist.
[SEG0069] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the X-ray before you leave, and I'll put a note on the water tablet that the dose doesn't match, so the chemist query is there.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks. Ask them which strength is on the last script, because now he's got me doubting myself, and I hate doubting myself.

[SEG0071] person_3 (DOCTOR): One more thing on the cousin. I'm not treating that as TB contact and I'm not throwing it out. If your brother has a letter or a name of a hospital, bring it, but I won't chase a story I can't verify today.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): He won't have a letter. He heard it off another cousin at a funeral. You know the way a story grows between the church and the car park.
[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then it stays unverified. The X-ray is for the cough you've actually got, not for a funeral story.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a relief, the way you put it. I was bracing for a lecture.
[SEG0075] person_3 (DOCTOR): No lecture. The wheeze is mild, the oxygen is fine, and a six-week cough after a flu still deserves a look. That's as far as I'll go.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I keep at the charity shop, or am I banjaxed until the film?
[SEG0077] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can keep the mornings if you feel up to it. If a shift wipes you, skip it. That's advice, not an order.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try Thursday and see. They've a sale on and they'll be stuck without me, which is flattering and a nuisance.
[SEG0079] person_1 (NURSE): Reception has you down for a fortnight from today, and the X-ray request is going through now.
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely. I'll bring the tablet box, and I won't google. Much.

spec.situation: Cough for six weeks after flu; worse at night; patient says no weight loss, then says clothes are loose; recent travel or TB contact denied by patient but a family member recalls a cousin's illness; doctor orders chest X-ray, avoids naming a cause.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: This is not family history; nurse reports possible cousin TB/contact story, not patient family medical history.
Current water tablet for blood pressure ~5 years is supported; bendroflumethiazide identity and exact regimen remain unresolved.
bad.text: water tablet (generic_name=bendroflumethiazide, frequency=once every morning, duration=approximately 5 years, indication=blood pressure, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Nurse will note mismatch; querying chemist about strength is suggested by patient, not clearly planned by nurse.
bad.text: Note the unmatched water-tablet dose and query the chemist about the strength (action_type=other, status=planned, responsible_person=nurse)

omissions.text: Medication dose discrepancy details are incomplete: repeat list showed bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg one each morning, patient first said she was certain she takes 5 mg, but later said she was only nearly sure and wondered if the box might be 2.5 mg tablets though she takes one tablet; doctor explicitly said the dose is not settled and he is not rewriting it today.
Cough is described as dry at night and worse at night, waking her husband.
Breathlessness is denied at rest; doctor advised urgent review if she becomes properly breathless at rest.
Patient initially denied weight loss ('I haven't lost weight') before later saying her trousers are loose and she may have dropped a bit.
No travel outside Clare except Limerick for Christmas shopping.

TB history is misrecorded as family history. What was actually said was an unverified possible contact/exposure story about cousin Aoife reportedly treated for TB in the spring, which the patient disputed; the doctor documented both versions and said he was not treating it as confirmed TB contact.
Exam summary also included that the lungs were clear overall except for a mild soft wheeze at the right base; doctor later stated the wheeze was mild and oxygen was fine.
Follow-up was specified as definite review in two weeks with the chest X-ray, whether she feels better or not.
Patient had nearly bought an over-the-counter cough bottle yesterday but did not take it.
